results.result: The study included 17 patients with adult-onset unilateral V1 damage (15 from stroke, 2 from tumor resection) and 9 age-matched controls. Patients averaged 54.9±14.4 years old with lesions occurring 45 months prior on average. All participants were matched by age and sex, with controls having normal vision and no neurological disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 and C148-C154 provide comprehensive demographic and inclusion criteria data that are internally consistent and clearly documented. The sample sizes, patient characteristics, and control matching are explicitly stated with appropriate detail for reproducibility.

results.result: Twelve patients were classified as blindsight positive and five as blindsight negative based on performance in a 2-AFC temporal detection task. Classification was validated using two independent cross-validation algorithms (k-nearest neighbors and Gaussian mixture model), both agreeing with the primary classification in all cases. No patients could describe stimuli in their blind field.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C29 describe the behavioral classification with appropriate validation. The use of two independent classification algorithms that agree in all cases (C29) provides strong methodological support. The behavioral criteria are clearly defined and the cross-validation approach is rigorous.

results.result: All 12 blindsight positive patients and all 9 controls showed intact ipsilateral LGN-hMT+ pathways with similar fascicle counts. The geniculate-hMT+ tract was reliably identified in all blindsight positive patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C22, C30-C32, and C103 are directly supported by tractography data in Table 1 and Figures 2-4. The consistency across all blindsight positive patients (12/12) and controls (9/9) provides strong evidence for this pathway's presence.

results.result: In blindsight negative patients, the LGN-hMT+ pathway was either untrackable (1/5 patients) or showed considerably impaired white matter microstructure (4/5 patients) compared to their intact hemisphere and controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C23, C34-C35 are supported by Table 1 and Figures 2-4 showing that 4/5 blindsight negative patients had trackable but abnormal pathways, while 1/5 (PN4) had no trackable pathway. The microstructural abnormalities are documented through FA and MD measurements.

results.result: Blindsight positive patients showed mean FA of 0.43±0.05 (damaged) vs 0.49±0.05 (intact) with 13.7% laterality, and MD of 0.81±0.07×10⁻³ (damaged) vs 0.73±0.05×10⁻³ (intact) with 9.6% laterality in the whole LGN-hMT+ tract. Blindsight negative patients showed more severe impairment: FA 0.35±0.1 (damaged) vs 0.47±0.03 (intact) with 34.7% laterality, and MD 1.05±0.22×10⁻³ (damaged) vs 0.77±0.05×10⁻³ (intact) with 27.0% laterality. Controls showed minimal laterality (3.3% FA, 1.6% MD).
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C45 provide detailed quantitative microstructural measurements that are internally consistent and supported by Figure 2B. The progressive pattern from controls (minimal laterality) to blindsight positive (moderate) to blindsight negative (severe) is coherent and well-documented.

results.result: Two-way ANOVA of the whole LGN-hMT+ tract showed no significant main effect of blindsight status on FA (F=2.6, p=0.13) but highly significant effects of lesion side (F=35.7, p<0.00005) and interaction (F=5.1, p=0.04). For MD, all effects were significant: blindsight status (F=9.2, p<0.01), lesion side (F=35.7, p<0.00005), and interaction (F=12.4, p<0.005).
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C51 report statistical analyses with appropriate test selection (two-way ANOVA) and clear reporting of F-statistics and p-values. The significant interaction effects support differential lesion impact between groups. However, the identical F-value for lesion side in both FA and MD analyses (F=35.7) is unusual and should be verified.

results.result: The LGN-hMT+ and LGN-V1 pathways frequently overlapped in their proximal portions (Figure 3A). The slight laterality in patients may be partially driven by overlap with degenerated optic radiations, as Wallerian degeneration would affect V1-projecting fibers throughout their course. The 2mm voxel resolution cannot distinguish between overlapping fiber bundles.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 identify an important confound and provide appropriate neurobiological reasoning (Wallerian degeneration, C54-C55) supported by citation. The technical limitation (C56) is accurately stated. This motivated the analysis of the distal tract portion to avoid contamination.

results.result: Analysis of the distal LGN-hMT+ tract portion (60-85% from LGN) showed reduced laterality in blindsight positive patients: FA 0.39±0.06 (damaged) vs 0.42±0.04 (intact), laterality 7.7%; MD laterality 7.6%. Blindsight negative patients maintained severe impairment: FA 0.29±0.07 (damaged) vs 0.44±0.05 (intact), laterality 51.7%; MD laterality 28.8%.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 show that analyzing the distal tract portion (avoiding overlap with optic radiations) reduces laterality in blindsight positive patients from 13.7% to 7.7% for FA, supporting the contamination hypothesis. Blindsight negative patients remain severely impaired, strengthening the conclusion that their pathway is truly damaged.

results.result: Two-way ANOVA of the distal LGN-hMT+ tract showed no significant effect of blindsight status on FA (F=0.7, p=0.42) but highly significant effects of lesion side (F=48.6, p<0.00001) and interaction (F=15.6, p<0.0005). For MD, all effects were significant: blindsight status (F=7.9, p=0.01), lesion side (F=31.4, p<0.0001), and interaction (F=15.6, p=0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C66 report appropriate statistical analyses for the distal tract portion. The pattern differs from the whole tract analysis, with stronger interaction effects. The identical F-value for the interaction in FA and MD (F=15.6) should be verified but could be coincidental.

results.result: Only blindsight negative patients possessed tracts in the damaged hemisphere that traversed regions of white matter with very abnormal FA and MD levels, as shown in Figure 4.
results.evaluation: Claim C67 is directly supported by Figure 4 showing that blindsight negative patients (PN1, PN5) have tracts passing through regions with markedly abnormal tissue properties, while blindsight positive patients (PB5, PB10) do not. This visual evidence complements the quantitative microstructure data.

results.result: Grey matter volume in hMT+ showed no significant effects of blindsight status (F=0.1, p=0.8), lesion side (F=1.7, p=0.2), or interaction (F=1.0, p=0.3), indicating that differences in hMT+ volume are unlikely to have affected the results.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 appropriately control for a potential confound (grey matter volume differences). The lack of significant effects and the inference that this is unlikely to affect results (C70) are justified by the statistical tests.

results.result: Alternative pathways showed variable presence across groups. Interhemispheric hMT+ tracts were present in only 6/12 blindsight positive patients, 1/5 blindsight negative patients, and 6/9 controls. Collicular-hMT+ pathways were present in 8/12 blindsight positive patients (damaged hemisphere), 3/5 blindsight negative patients, and 9/9 controls (left) or 7/9 (right).
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7 and C71-C72, C80-C82 are directly supported by Table 1. The variable presence of these pathways across all groups, including their absence in some blindsight positive patients and presence in some blindsight negative patients, argues against their necessity for blindsight.

results.result: Interhemispheric hMT+ pathways crossed via the corpus callosum as expected. Where present in blindsight positive patients, mean FA was 0.64±0.07 and MD 0.70±0.03×10⁻³, similar to controls (FA 0.64±0.07, MD 0.67±0.05×10⁻³). The single blindsight negative patient (PN2) with this pathway showed intact microstructure (FA=0.59, MD=0.73×10⁻³, within control range).
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C79 show that when interhemispheric pathways are present, they appear intact even in one blindsight negative patient (PN2). This further argues against this pathway's necessity for blindsight. The anatomical route via corpus callosum (C73) is consistent with known anatomy.

results.result: Collicular-hMT+ pathways in blindsight positive patients showed FA 0.40±0.05 (damaged) vs 0.46±0.03 (intact), laterality 13.9%; MD 0.78±0.08×10⁻³ vs 0.69±0.04×10⁻³, laterality 10.8%. Blindsight negative patients showed FA 0.37±0.05 (damaged) vs 0.42±0.03 (intact), laterality 14.0%. Two blindsight negative patients (PN2, PN3) showed similar collicular tract microstructure in both hemispheres despite impaired LGN-hMT+ pathways. No significant difference in ipsilesional FA or MD between groups (FA: t=0.9, p=0.4; MD: t=0.8, p=0.45).
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C90 show that collicular pathways can be intact in blindsight negative patients (C89), and there's no significant difference between groups (C90). This argues against the collicular pathway being necessary for blindsight. The statistical comparisons are appropriate though limited by small sample sizes.

results.result: Correlation between behavioral performance and distal LGN-hMT+ tract microstructure was in the predicted direction but not significant (FA: r=0.44, p=0.09; MD: r=-0.48, p=0.06). Neither collicular-hMT+ (FA: r=-0.03, p=0.93; MD: r=-0.10, p=0.77) nor interhemispheric hMT+ (FA: r=-0.33, p=0.39; MD: r=0.26, p=0.50) tracts showed any correlation with behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 report correlations that approach but do not reach significance for the LGN-hMT+ tract (p=0.09 and p=0.06). The authors acknowledge insufficient power. The lack of correlation for alternative pathways (C93) supports their lesser role, but the marginal p-values for the main pathway leave the relationship uncertain. Larger sample sizes would be needed to definitively establish this relationship.

results.result: Blindsight negative patients had larger lesions (36,923±23,035 mm³) than blindsight positive patients (13,461±7,101 mm³), approximately 2.5 times larger on average. There was a significant correlation between occipital lobe damage extent and ipsilesional LGN-hMT+ pathway microstructure (FA: r=-0.59, p=0.015; MD: r=0.63, p=0.01).
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 show that lesion size differs between groups and correlates with pathway integrity. This is important for understanding the mechanism: larger lesions are more likely to damage the LGN-hMT+ pathway. The significant correlations (C97) support the relationship between lesion extent and pathway damage.

results.result: There was no clear association between blindsight function and non-occipital damage. Only one patient (PN5) showed significant subcortical pathology affecting LGN and pulvinar. At least three blindsight positive patients (PB1, PB4, PB10) had complete calcarine cortex destruction, while some blindsight negative patients (PN2, PN4) had small V1 regions apparently intact.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C101 show that complete V1 destruction is not incompatible with blindsight (C100), and partial V1 sparing doesn't guarantee it (C101). The minimal subcortical involvement (C99) suggests cortical pathways are more important. These observations support the focus on white matter pathways rather than grey matter sparing.

results.result: The study concludes that blindsight may be facilitated by an intact LGN-hMT+ pathway, with preservation or destruction of this tract predicting presence or absence of blindsight. Intact LGN-hMT+ connections may be both sufficient (since all blindsight positive patients had them) and necessary (since no blindsight negative patients had intact connections) for blindsight function in adult-onset V1 damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C21, C107-C108, and C143 represent the main conclusions. These are well-supported by the convergent evidence: (1) 100% of blindsight positive patients had intact pathways; (2) 0% of blindsight negative patients had intact pathways; (3) alternative pathways were inconsistent; (4) microstructural measures distinguished groups. The sufficiency claim (C107) is strong; the necessity claim (C108) is qualified by acknowledging unexplored pathways.

results.result: Alternative candidate tracts (collicular-hMT+ and interhemispheric hMT+) showed variable presence in both patient groups and are unlikely to have a major role in blindsight function. These pathways were absent or impaired in some blindsight positive patients but intact in some blindsight negative patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25, C110-C112, and C144-C145 conclude that alternative pathways are unlikely to underlie blindsight. This is supported by: (1) absence in some blindsight positive patients; (2) presence in some blindsight negative patients; (3) lack of correlation with behavior; (4) much lower fascicle counts than LGN-hMT+ pathway. The logic is sound and data-driven.

results.result: The study identified a significant methodological concern: it was possible to track fascicles through regions of extremely impaired FA and MD in patients. Patient PN1 showed 10× more fascicles in the damaged hemisphere despite tracts passing through abnormal tissue. Fascicle numbers are unreliable measures of true axonal projections due to tract length, curvature, and branching. Even controls showed notable inter-hemispheric and inter-individual variability in fascicle counts.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C138 identify an important limitation of tractography methods. The observation that PN1 had more fascicles in the damaged hemisphere (C133) despite non-functional pathways (C134) demonstrates the problem. The citations to methodological literature (C136-C137) support that this is a known issue. This critically important finding validates the study's emphasis on microstructure over fascicle counts.

results.result: The results highlight the importance of considering white matter microstructure when performing tractography in patients, applicable to anyone working with clinical diffusion data.
results.evaluation: Claim C146 is a methodological conclusion strongly supported by the demonstration that fascicle counts alone are insufficient (trackable pathways in PN1 were non-functional). The study's approach of combining tractography with FA/MD analysis along tract profiles provides a model for future work.

results.result: There was considerable variation in fascicle numbers between participants (controls: 19-653; patients: 17-635) and between hemispheres, as expected from prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claim C33 documents expected variability in fascicle counts, supported by citations to Jones et al., 2013 and Pestilli et al., 2014. This variability is similar between controls and patients, suggesting it reflects methodological factors rather than pathology per se.

results.result: False positive connections are particularly problematic in tractography. A less stringent cleaning threshold would suggest collicular tracts in all blindsight positive patients, but pathways with <5 fascicles appear largely implausible when visualized. Linear Fascicle Evaluation may help estimate connectome accuracy in future studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C142 discuss the challenge of false positives and the importance of cleaning thresholds. The observation that <5 fascicle pathways appear implausible (C141) justifies the cleaning approach. The suggestion of Linear Fascicle Evaluation (C142) is appropriately cited as a future direction.

results.result: V1 damage causes hemianopia, but many patients retain residual vision (blindsight). Over 30 years, several pathways have been proposed to underlie blindsight, but the relative roles and neurobiological bases remained unknown prior to this study. The necessary circuitry supporting preserved vision after V1 damage had not been identified.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C11, and C18 establish the background and knowledge gap. These are appropriately supported by citations (particularly Cowey, 2010 review) and accurately represent the state of the field. The claim that necessary circuitry was unidentified (C18) is justified and motivates the study.

results.result: Prior work established that dMRI with tractography can estimate white matter tracts non-invasively. Previous studies proposed three candidate pathways for blindsight: (1) LGN-hMT+ connections, (2) interhemispheric plasticity, and (3) superior colliculus/pulvinar connections to hMT+. The macaque LGN can support residual visual processing after V1 lesion.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C17 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. The three proposed mechanisms are correctly attributed to previous work (de Gelder et al., 2008; Bridge et al., 2010; Leh et al., 2006; Warner et al., 2010, 2015). The macaque evidence (C14) provides comparative support.

results.result: This is the first study to perform dMRI tractography comparing microstructural properties of visual pathways in V1-damaged patients categorized by blindsight function. The findings are consistent with the authors' recent fMRI study and with macaque neuroanatomy showing direct LGN-hMT+ connections.
results.evaluation: Claims C102, C104-C106 establish the study's novelty and consistency with prior work. The claim of being the first such study (C102) appears justified given the literature review. Consistency with the authors' fMRI work (C104, Ajina et al., 2015a) and macaque anatomy (C105-C106, Sincich et al., 2004) strengthens the findings.

results.result: The study acknowledges limitations: other unexplored pathways could underlie blindsight in blindsight negative patients; alternative pathways may still contribute in some circumstances; the study cannot completely rule out an intact pulvinar-hMT+ pathway due to resolution limitations.
results.evaluation: Claims C109, C113, and C118 appropriately acknowledge study limitations. The caveat about unexplored pathways (C109) is important for interpreting the necessity claim. The pulvinar limitation (C118) is particularly important given the known pulvinar-MT connections in primates.

results.result: The pulvinar pathway to hMT+ exists as either a di-synaptic route via inferior pulvinar (from colliculus) or a direct retinorecipient pathway. A recent human tractography study found LGN-hMT+ and pulvinar-hMT+ tracts were very similar with almost identical FA and MD values. At 2mm resolution, dissecting these tracts may be impossible due to thalamic structure proximity.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C117 explain why the pulvinar pathway wasn't separately analyzed. The reasoning is sound: (1) the collicular-pulvinar-hMT+ pathway was tested; (2) prior work (Allen et al., 2015) showed LGN and pulvinar pathways are indistinguishable at this resolution; (3) the technical limitation is acknowledged. This is an important caveat for interpretation.

results.result: Previous case studies (patient GY, hemispherectomy patients) showed unusual connectivity patterns possibly indicating plasticity, including strengthened interhemispheric connections. The current study found no evidence for such plasticity in adult-onset V1 damage. Age of injury onset may explain differences, as childhood damage may lead to greater plasticity, and the corpus callosum continues growing until early adulthood.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C127 appropriately contextualize differences from prior case studies. The age-of-onset hypothesis (C124) is reasonable and supported by developmental neuroscience citations (Anderson et al., 2011; Tinelli et al., 2013; Keshavan et al., 2002). The lack of plasticity in adult-onset cases (C122) is supported by the data showing no unusual patterns.

results.result: Different forms of blindsight may be mediated by distinct anatomical pathways. Collicular processing may be involved in 'action' or 'attention' blindsight, while the LGN is implicated in perceptual characteristics ('agnosopsia').
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C130 discuss the possibility that different blindsight types have different substrates, appropriately citing Danckert and Rossetti, 2005 and Zeki and Ffytche, 1998. This provides context for why the current study's focus on perceptual detection may have found LGN-hMT+ to be critical while other studies emphasized collicular pathways.

results.result: Appreciation of the important tracts may help direct attempts to boost residual function through rehabilitative strategies in hemianopia.
results.evaluation: Claim C147 speculates about clinical applications. While identifying the critical pathway is a necessary first step for targeted rehabilitation, the study provides no data on rehabilitation outcomes. This remains a reasonable but untested hypothesis requiring future work.
